newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Gloomy Bulgarians vote for new president.
newsitem.headline: Gloomy Bulgarians vote for new president.

text.p: Bulgarians, mired in the legacy of communism and facing further hardship this winter, voted for a new president on Sunday -- with few expecting any early change for the better.

The spectre of bread and fuel shortages hung over polling stations throughout the country, from the Romanian border in the north to the Black Sea in the east and the southern frontiers with Greece and Turkey.

The reform laggard of the former Soviet Warsaw Pact countries, this largely agricultural nation of just 8.4 million people was holding its second presidential election since the fall of communism in 1989.
After a slow start, turnout was brisk as most of the country basked in bright Autumn sunshine.

A big defeat for the candidate of the ruling Socialist party, Culture Minister Ivan Marazov, could be deeply embarrassing for the government of Prime Minister Zhan Videnov, already under fire for dragging its feet on reform.
Many voters said they were supporting the main opposition candidate, lawyer Petar Stoyanov, but the Socialists retain a faithful following of mostly elderly voters.
The last opinion poll gave Stoyanov 32.5 percent of the vote and Marazov 21.5 percent.

Pensioner Ana Georgieva, voting in central Sofia, recalled the free education her sons enjoyed under former dictator Todor Zhivkov, who was ousted in 1989, and said her family could not afford to send her granddaughter to university.
"Everything went to ruins in 1989," Georgieva said. "And you call this democracy."

Many of Bulgaria's two million pensioners are nostalgic for the greater security offered by one-party rule, when Zhivkov's state ensured food was cheap, even though freedom of speech and movement were restricted.
Outsiders like George Ganchev, the colourful head of the Bulgarian Business Bloc who traditionally attracts protest votes, won significant support in working class areas.

"I'll vote for Ganchev because he is the only one who can deal with crime," said an engineer outside the imposing Stalinist-style House of the Metallurgists in the industrial town of Pernik, 30 km (18 miles) southwest of Sofia.

Workers turning out to vote beneath the smokestacks of the Stomana steelworks said they had lost faith in politicians. "They are all the same, they just change their seats," said a Ganchev supporter aged about 50 who gave his name as Dimiter.
"We will vote for Ganchev and most of the workers we know will also vote for him. A mad country needs a mad president," said Stoyan Ivanov, 35.
Bulgarians are voting in 55 countries abroad, mainly in North America and Western Europe, and polling stations are also set up at prisons, mental hospitals and clinics.

Polls close at 7 p.m. (1700 GMT) and preliminary results are expected early on Monday. If no one wins more than half the votes, or if turnout is below 50 percent, a second round will be held next Sunday.

While most other ex-Soviet east European satellites have seen some benefits from economic reform and are pressing for inclusion in NATO and the European Union, Bulgaria remains largely unable or unwilling to shake off the last vestiges of communism.

An ambitious privatisation programme remains largely stalled in the face of powerful vested interests while several foreign investors privately complain Sofia still looks more to Moscow for inspiration than Brussels.
It has the lowest level of outside investment of any country in the region and a quarter of its numerous and insolvent banks are in receivership.

Foreign exchange reserves have plunged to about $505 million from $1.5 billion a year ago and the government is looking to an International Monetary Fund mission due on Wednesday to release a twice-delayed $115 million credit and stave off default on the country's foreign debt.
